title: Agentic AI for a $12.4B Banking Enterprise
summary: Owning a $6.4M Agentic AI portfolio and building a multi-product AI platform - Chat Agents, Voice Agents, Lending AI, Requirement Gathering, Spend Intelligence and Risk Intelligence - for a $12.4 billion U.S. banking enterprise.
challenge: A banking enterprise ran high-volume, low-efficiency manual processes that couldn't be automated with rules. The work required judgement, document context and conversational handling - but under HIPAA, PCI-DSS and GDPR obligations, with executive scrutiny on accuracy and latency.
research: 4+ process discovery workshops with business stakeholders documented current-state workflows, surfaced operational bottlenecks and defined optimisation opportunities before any model decision was made.
discovery: Discovery separated processes into three buckets: deterministic (automate conventionally), context-heavy (RAG), and conversation-driven (agentic). That segmentation set the platform architecture and the product roadmap.
prioritization: Sequenced by risk-adjusted value: highest-volume manual processes with the clearest evaluation criteria shipped first, so accuracy could be proven before expanding surface area.
roadmap: 0→1 Chat Agents on the highest-volume support surface
Enterprise RAG pipelines with Model Context Protocol integration
Knowledge graph layer for cross-document reasoning
Voice Agents for realtime workflows
Lending AI, Spend Intelligence and Risk Intelligence expansion
1→N scaling across business units
userStories: As an operations analyst, I need the agent to resolve routine requests end to end so my queue holds only exceptions.
As a compliance officer, I need every AI decision auditable against HIPAA, PCI-DSS and GDPR obligations.
As an executive sponsor, I need accuracy, latency and uptime reported continuously, not anecdotally.
As a risk analyst, I need spend and risk signals surfaced from documents I would otherwise read manually.
architecture: Enterprise-grade RAG pipelines - semantic, hybrid, self, memory and graph retrieval
Model Context Protocol platform and servers connecting agents to enterprise systems
Knowledge graph introduced for cross-source reasoning
LLM evaluation and observability with Langfuse, Grafana and Promptfoo red-teaming
Architecture Review Board release governance gating every deployment
launch: Released under ARB-compliant governance at 95% adherence, with compliance sign-off across HIPAA, PCI-DSS and GDPR for every AI deployment.
failures: Early iterations proved that model quality alone doesn't survive enterprise scrutiny - without a formal evaluation harness, accuracy claims couldn't be defended to the ARB. Red-teaming with Promptfoo exposed failure modes that hadn't appeared in happy-path testing.
lessons: Evaluation infrastructure is a launch requirement, not a post-launch nicety
Governance participation early converts the ARB from a gate into an accelerator
Agentic scope should expand only after the previous surface holds its accuracy SLA
retrospective: The portfolio scaled because evaluation, observability and governance were treated as first-class product surfaces. Team structure followed: an 8+ member cross-functional organisation with 3 PMs, 3 developers, 1 QA and 1 designer, restructured on Agile to lift release velocity 30%.

title: 26 Products, ₹7.78 Cr: Building an Enterprise SaaS Category
summary: Category ownership across Enterprise SaaS, Consumer Tech and Fintech - 26 products, ₹7.78 Cr revenue, and an 82% enterprise retention improvement.
challenge: A broad portfolio of fintech and SaaS products competed for the same delivery capacity, with enterprise customers churning after onboarding friction and no shared roadmap discipline across the category.
research: Analysed retention cohorts against onboarding duration and integration complexity to locate where enterprise accounts actually disengaged.
discovery: Onboarding - not features - was the churn driver. Enterprise accounts that cleared integration quickly retained; those that stalled during API setup never recovered.
stakeholders: Enterprise customers and their technical teams
prioritization: Roadmap balanced strategic company priorities against direct customer value, with onboarding-path work protected from feature-request pressure.
roadmap: Instrument the enterprise onboarding funnel
Optimise API-driven integrations
UX rework of the onboarding workflow with the UX team
GTM programme for enterprise SaaS adoption
Agile restructuring across 5 delivery teams
userStories: As an enterprise buyer, I need integration to complete in days so value lands inside the evaluation window.
As a customer success manager, I need visibility into where an account is stuck in onboarding.
As a delivery lead, I need one prioritised category backlog rather than 26 competing ones.
architecture: API-driven integration layer standardised across products
launch: Rolled out through sprint ceremonies across 5 cross-functional teams, with Agile mentoring to sustain the change after launch.
failures: Treating each product's roadmap independently early on spread delivery capacity too thin; the category only moved once prioritisation was consolidated.
lessons: Retention is an onboarding metric long before it is a feature metric
Category ownership means saying no across products, not optimising within one
Agile mentoring outlasts Agile mandates
retrospective: Consolidating prioritisation and attacking onboarding produced an 82% retention improvement and a 35% reduction in onboarding time - outcomes no individual feature roadmap would have delivered.

title: Cutting B2B Churn 22% Through UX-Led Redesign
summary: Launching an enterprise B2B eCommerce platform, improving vendor onboarding 29% and cutting churn 22% through UX-led design improvements, while lifting lead conversion 18% via CRM integration.
challenge: Vendors abandoned onboarding partway through, and enterprise accounts churned after the first cycle. Sales and product were also working from disconnected lead data.
research: Onboarding drop-off analysis by step, paired with vendor interviews on where the process lost them.
discovery: Vendor onboarding failed on comprehension, not capability - the steps existed but the sequence and language didn't match how vendors think about listing.
prioritization: Onboarding sequence rework first (highest churn leverage), CRM integration second (highest revenue leverage).
roadmap: Instrument onboarding step-level drop-off
Resequence and rewrite the onboarding flow
Enterprise CRM integration
GTM alignment between product marketing and sales execution
userStories: As a vendor, I need to understand what each onboarding step requires before I start it.
As a sales rep, I need enterprise lead activity in the CRM without manual entry.
As an enterprise buyer, I need the platform to hold my catalogue structure, not flatten it.
architecture: B2B eCommerce platform with vendor-scoped catalogue management
CRM integration for enterprise lead flow
launch: Launched with GTM strategies aligning product marketing to sales execution, so the funnel and the product moved together.
failures: The first onboarding revision added explanatory content without changing the sequence - it barely moved the numbers. The resequencing did.
lessons: Explaining a bad flow is not the same as fixing it
CRM integration is a product feature when sales is part of the funnel
retrospective: UX-led design work - not incentives or feature additions - delivered the 22% churn reduction, which reset how the team scoped retention work afterwards.

title: Predictive Credit Risk at Enterprise Scale
summary: Building predictive credit risk models for enterprise financial services - 15% accuracy improvement - and the real-time dashboards that made them actionable across 25+ KPIs.
challenge: Credit risk decisions relied on models whose outputs never reached the executives making portfolio calls, and accuracy plateaued below what the business needed.
research: Feature analysis across the credit portfolio alongside stakeholder interviews on which risk signals actually influenced decisions.
discovery: The gap was distribution, not modelling: risk signals existed but had no executive-facing surface, so decisions ran on stale reporting.
prioritization: Model accuracy and dashboard delivery advanced in parallel - accuracy alone would not have changed a single decision.
roadmap: Predictive credit risk model development
Accuracy improvement iterations
Real-time analytics dashboards across 25+ KPIs
Translation of business requirements into analytical solutions
userStories: As a risk executive, I need portfolio risk visible in real time, not in a monthly pack.
As an analyst, I need model outputs traceable to the features that drove them.
architecture: Real-time analytics dashboards tracking 25+ business and operational KPIs
launch: Deployed as an executive-visible dashboard layer over the risk models, with cross-functional stakeholder alignment on definitions.
failures: Early dashboards mirrored the model's internal structure rather than the executive decision - they were accurate and unused until reframed around decisions.
lessons: A model that doesn't reach a decision-maker has zero accuracy in practice
Dashboard structure should mirror decisions, not data models
retrospective: This engagement set the data-driven decision-making pattern carried into every later product role: instrument the decision, then improve the model.

title: Lenskart: Virtual Try-On and AI Personalization
summary: Research case study on how Lenskart improved online eyewear shopping with AR virtual try-on, AI recommendations and a streamlined returns experience to lift conversion, reduce returns and grow loyalty.
challenge: Traditional eyewear shopping was limited by store selection and time-consuming store visits, while online buyers faced uncertainty without trying frames on. Lenskart saw ~30% churn among new users, ~20% online return rates, and an estimated $2M annual revenue loss from dissatisfied customers.
research: Surveyed 10,000+ customers, ran focus groups, and conducted one-on-one interviews with frequent eyewear buyers. Research showed 65% struggled to pick frames online, 45% disliked the return process, and 55% wanted personalization they were not getting.
discovery: Discovery framed the problem as an experience gap: buyers needed confidence before purchase. Competitive analysis of Warby Parker and Zenni Optical plus market growth in AR try-on pointed to virtual try-on, AI recommendations and simpler returns as the highest-leverage bets.
stakeholders: End customers across age and style segments
prioritization: Used MoSCoW and an impact-vs-effort matrix. Must-haves: virtual try-on, AI personalized recommendations, and a streamlined return process. Supporting catalog and UX improvements followed.
roadmap: Ship AR virtual try-on for frame confidence
Launch AI-driven personalized frame recommendations
Simplify the returns and exchange flow
Expand catalog and mobile experience
Iterate on retention loops using engagement and NPS signals
userStories: As an online shopper, I want to virtually try frames on my face so I can buy with confidence.
As a returning customer, I want personalized suggestions so I do not browse endlessly.
As a dissatisfied buyer, I want a simple return flow so a wrong fit does not end the relationship.
architecture: AI recommendation layer using preferences and facial cues
launch: Rolled out as a research-backed product narrative covering try-on, personalization and returns as one coherent shopping journey rather than isolated features.
failures: Without try-on and personalization, online acquisition leaked into returns and churn. Treating returns as an ops afterthought amplified cost and dissatisfaction.
lessons: Confidence features can outperform pure catalog expansion for conversion
Personalization only compounds after the try-before-you-buy friction is removed
Return experience is a growth lever, not just a cost center
retrospective: This Notion research case study shows how AR + AI personalization can turn a high-uncertainty category into a measurable retention and revenue engine.

title: Amazon miniTV: Free, Snackable OTT Growth in India
summary: Research case study on Amazon miniTV's growth strategy in India's OTT market - using a free ad-supported model, Amazon ecosystem distribution, snackable content and creator partnerships to reach 60M+ MAUs.
challenge: India's OTT market was dominated by paid giants like Netflix, Hotstar and Prime Video. Price-sensitive and first-time streamers were blocked by subscriptions, leaving an underserved audience Amazon could capture with a free offering.
research: Analyzed value propositions of miniTV vs Prime Video, price sensitivity in India, and the role of short-form consumption habits. Focused on how free access could act as a gateway into the broader Amazon ecosystem.
discovery: Discovery centered on a new audience segment rather than competing head-on for paying subscribers: remove the paywall, distribute inside Amazon, and win attention with snackable creator-led content.
stakeholders: Price-sensitive and first-time streamers in India
prioritization: Prioritized free access, in-app Amazon distribution, short-form formats, data-led curation and creator partnerships over big-budget prestige originals.
roadmap: Launch free AVOD experience inside Amazon
Seed snackable short-form series and comedy
Partner with digital creators for cost-efficient supply
Use viewing data to curate retention loops
Convert engaged free users toward Amazon ecosystem depth
userStories: As a price-sensitive viewer, I want free on-demand shows so entertainment is not gated by a subscription.
As a busy user, I want short episodes I can finish in a commute or break.
As Amazon, I want miniTV discovery inside shopping flows so acquisition stays cheap.
launch: Positioned as a free growth wedge in a paid OTT market, with comedy, short thrillers and light drama as early engagement formats.
kpis: ~45 minutes average watch time per session
Strong engagement in comedy / short thrillers / light drama
failures: Competing only with premium subscriptions would have excluded the largest incremental audience. Ignoring snackable formats would have missed mobile-first attention windows.
lessons: Free can be a deliberate acquisition and funnel strategy, not just a giveaway
Distribution inside an existing super-app beats cold-start marketing
Format-market fit matters as much as catalogue size
retrospective: This Notion research case study frames miniTV as a product-growth play: remove payment friction, ride Amazon distribution, and win with short-form relevance.

title: Gumroad: Why Creators Choose Direct Digital Commerce
summary: Research case study on Gumroad's product and growth strategy - simple creator tools, direct storefronts and flexible monetization that helped the platform scale to $200M+ GMV and profitability.
challenge: Creators struggled to sell digital goods directly without the complexity of Shopify-like setups or the marketplace dilution of Etsy. Acquisition, feature bloat, compliance and scale pressure made simple monetization hard.
research: Studied Gumroad's founding thesis, fee model, creator tooling, and competitive alternatives. Mapped why creators preferred a lightweight direct-sales path over heavy e-commerce stacks.
discovery: The winning wedge was simplicity and creator empowerment: custom storefronts, analytics, flexible pricing and low operational overhead, grown through content and social channels.
prioritization: Prioritized simplicity, flexible monetization and creator analytics over feature parity with full e-commerce platforms. Growth goals included GMV, fee revenue, premium MRR and MAU expansion.
roadmap: Ship a frictionless creator storefront
Add analytics and flexible pricing
Grow via content and social distribution
Introduce subscriptions / premium layers
Optimize load time, mobile usability and satisfaction
userStories: As a creator, I want to sell digital products quickly without building a full store.
As a seller, I want clear analytics so I know what converts.
As Gumroad, I want fee and subscription revenue that scales with creator success.
launch: Public in 2012, scaled through creator word-of-mouth and tooling depth, reaching $200M+ GMV by 2016 and profitability by 2020.
failures: Chasing full Shopify/Etsy feature parity would have destroyed the simplicity wedge. Ignoring mobile and load performance would have capped creator conversion.
lessons: For creators, time-to-first-sale beats platform richness
Fee models should stay aligned with creator success
Growth goals only work when tied to UX and performance work
retrospective: This Notion research case study highlights Gumroad as a product of restraint: win creators with simplicity, then compound with analytics and monetization layers.

title: Astrotalk: Why Astrology Commerce Is Winning in India
summary: Research case study on Astrotalk's traction in India - cultural affinity, vetted experts, mobile convenience, freemium first-chat and focus on marriage, relationships and career for 25-35 year olds.
challenge: Online astrology and tarot were not new, yet trust, skepticism and timing still blocked mass adoption. The question was why Astrotalk was gaining traction now, not whether the category existed.
research: Analyzed founding narrative, cultural context in India, audience demographics (Similarweb), freemium conversion mechanics, and category resurgence among millennials and Gen Z amid uncertainty and social influence.
discovery: Success came from packaging a traditional behavior for modern mobile life: credible astrologers, privacy, 24/7 access, freemium first chat, and high-intent topics like marriage, relationships and career.
prioritization: Prioritized trust (astrologer vetting + privacy), convenience (mobile 24/7), freemium onboarding, and category focus on high-stakes life decisions over generic horoscope content.
roadmap: Build trusted astrologer marketplace with privacy controls
Ship mobile-first 24/7 consultation experience
Use freemium first chat to convert skeptics
Concentrate supply on marriage, relationships and career
Expand internationally while deepening India cultural fit
userStories: As a busy urban user, I want astrological guidance on my phone without booking an in-person visit.
As a skeptic, I want a free first chat so I can judge value before paying.
As a privacy-conscious user, I want my birth details protected.
launch: Grew from a culturally resonant India thesis into a multi-country mobile marketplace, with renewed traction as interest in astrology rose among younger users.
kpis: Strong demand in marriage / relationships / career consultations
failures: Generic horoscope content and weak trust signals fail in a skepticism-heavy category. Without freemium, first-time conversion stays blocked.
lessons: Cultural affinity is a distribution advantage when paired with modern UX
Trust and privacy are product features in sensitive categories
Freemium is especially powerful when belief and willingness-to-pay are uncertain
retrospective: This Notion research case study shows Astrotalk winning by modernizing a trusted cultural behavior rather than inventing a new one.
